_comment: The contract between ProgressionLedger.cs and functions/src/progression.ts.
Earned currency is derived twice on purpose: the client derives it so the game
works offline, and the server derives it so a forged save can be caught rather
than merely disbelieved. Two implementations of one rule will drift — this file is
what makes the drift fail a test instead of quietly desynchronising money.
firebase/functions/test/reward-vectors.mjs. Change the arithmetic on either side
and add a vector proving what changed.
'credits' is checked by both sides. 'xp' is checked only by the client, because XP
has no economic effect and the server has no reason to compute it.
Shapes are chosen so Unity's JsonUtility can read the file too: arrays of objects
rather than maps, since JsonUtility cannot deserialise a dictionary.

_dailyComment: The contract between DailyChestTable.cs and functions/src/daily.ts.
A daily chest's contents are rolled twice: by the client so the reward can be
shown and spent offline, and by the server so the grant can be adjudicated
without believing the client's number. Two implementations of one generator will
drift, and the symptom would be a player watching a balance change after a sync.
The config below is synthetic, not the shipped table. What is under test is the
algorithm — the hash, the shift amounts, the stream numbers, the modulo and the
merging of same-kind drops — so retuning the real drop rates must not turn these
red. Change any of that arithmetic on either side and add a vector proving what
changed; every unopened chest in the world is rerolled by it.
_goldenComment: The contract between GoldenBonus.cs and functions/src/progression.ts.
A glade's golden multiplier is a pure function of (account id, level id): the client
uses it to show what a clear was worth, and the server re-derives the same number when
it recomputes earned credits. Neither side tells the other. If they disagree, a player
watches their balance change after a sync, which is the worst thing an economy can do
Everything behind it is contract: the FNV basis and prime, the xorshift shifts, the
'golden' tag, the stream number 0, the plain modulo, and the order the bands are
walked in. Changing any of them re-rolls every glade in the world.
An empty player key pays 100 — no bonus. That is the state before the first sign-in,
and paying the base is the only direction that cannot cost anybody anything.
_streakComment: The contract between StreakTable.cs and functions/src/streak.ts.
The streak ladder pays currency, so what a night is worth is decided twice: the client
shows it and the server grants it, from its own copy published to config/progression.
A disagreement means a player watches a reward arrive as a different number from the
one the board promised — the same failure the chest vectors exist to prevent.
Two things are under contract here and neither is obvious. The ladder *laps*: night
eight pays night one's rung, for ever, because a streak has no end and a ladder does.
And the per-kind ceilings are shared — a rung authored above one is clamped to the same
figure on both sides, so a content file that overreaches produces one number, not two.
The ladder below is synthetic and deliberately unlike the shipped one: what is under
contract is the lookup, not this season's rewards. Nights 6 and 7 are authored above
the credit and gem ceilings on purpose, so the clamp is pinned rather than assumed.
The `advances` rule that bounds a claim has no client half — the client never judges
its own claim — so it is not pinned here. It is tested in functions/test.

_eventComment: The contract between EventLedger.cs and functions/src/progression.ts.
An event's progress is a count of its glades whose *first* clear falls inside its
window, and its reward is the milestones that count has passed. Both sides derive it
from records the catalog vouches for — nothing is claimed, granted or stored — so the
reward simply becomes part of the earned credits the server already recomputes.
Two rules the cases pin, because a naive implementation gets them wrong: a clear dated
outside the window counts for nothing however many stars it has, and a level the
catalog does not know advances no event.
